43.title: A basket on the river
43.hook: Musa's mother is inspired to set her baby on the Nile, and not to fear
43.howItsDone: Muslims retell the story of Musa's mother as a model of trust in Allah (tawakkul), and her story in Surah al-Qasas is often recited and taught to children.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Ka'ba, and a father and son asking only that their work be accepted. Your line was accept it from us. Now, two weeks with Musa and Pharaoh.

The first day of school. The car keys. The airport gate. Parents hold on as long as they can, and then they open their hands. Now take that to Egypt, long ago. Pharaoh has split the land into factions, and one people, the Children of Israel, he treats as the weak ones: their baby boys are being killed. A woman among them has just given birth to a son. She's nursing him, hiding him, listening for footsteps. Then she is given an instruction that sounds like the opposite of everything a mother knows.

Musa, peace be upon him, comes back again and again in the Qur'an, in pieces across many surahs. This piece is in Surah al-Qasas, the Stories. Allah inspired the mother of Musa: nurse him. And when you fear for him, cast him into the river, and do not fear, and do not grieve. We will bring him back to you and make him one of the messengers. Look at the order. First: nurse him. Hold him while you can. Then, when the fear comes, not before: the water. And two things forbidden to her: fear and grief. Not because there's nothing to fear, but because two promises have been made. He'll come back to you. And he'll be a messenger. The Qur'an calls this wahy, inspiration, the same word used for revelation to prophets, though scholars explain that for her it was inspiration placed in the heart, not prophecy. A small surprise: the Qur'an's own word for what she used isn't basket. In Surah Ta-Ha it's tabut, a chest or box. The basket of reeds is how Exodus tells it. Either way, a mother closes a lid over her baby and sets him on the Nile. Most of what we'll hear about Musa is big: fire, staffs, a sea. It begins here, with a woman opening her hands at the edge of a river, because she trusted what she had been told more than what she feared.

segments.voice: Find the worry you've been nursing; her order was nurse him first, then the river, so first name the one thing you can still do about it today. Then close the lid on the rest and set it on a slow, wide river, into Allah's hands, or, if that's not your language, just out of your own; you're not forgetting it, just trusting the river with the part you can't carry. If you pray, name it as you let it go.
Tabut, the chest that carried baby Musa onto the Nile.
Your line: put it on the river. Two promises went down the river with him. Day forty-three.

44.title: Asiya's arms
44.hook: Pharaoh's wife finds the baby and says: a joy for me and you, do not kill him
44.carry: a good heart in a hard house
44.howItsDone: Muslims honor Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh, as a woman of faith the Qur'an itself holds up as an example, and some recite her prayer from Surah at-Tahrim in times of hardship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tabut, the chest on the river, and a mother opening her hands at the water's edge. Your line was put it on the river.

A gentle parent raised by a harsh one. A coworker who stays decent in an office where nobody else bothers. Kindness doesn't always come from the house a person is in; sometimes they carry it in themselves. The river carries the chest downstream, and where does it wash up? Of all the places in Egypt, at Pharaoh's own palace. His household lifts it from the water. Inside is a baby boy, exactly the kind Pharaoh has ordered killed. Then a woman steps forward, between the baby and the man who gives the orders.
screen: `KINDNESS FROM A HARD HOUSE.` → `THE CHEST REACHES THE PALACE.` → `A WOMAN STEPS FORWARD.`

segments.voice: Surah al-Qasas again. Pharaoh's household picks the baby up, and his wife says: a delight of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him. Perhaps he will be of use to us, or we may take him as a son. Delight of the eye is qurratu 'ayn, literally coolness of the eye. One old explanation: in a hot land, a cool eye is a happy one, resting on something it loves. She looks at a baby her husband has sentenced to death, calls him her delight to his face, and adds: do not kill him. The Qur'an doesn't give her name. Muslim tradition calls her Asiya, and honors her. Her faith shows up later, in Surah at-Tahrim, where the Qur'an holds her up as an example for believers. She prays: my Lord, build for me a home with You in the Garden, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds. The queen of Egypt, in a palace, asking for a different house. And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in a hadith in Bukhari, named her among the women who reached perfection, alongside Maryam, the mother of 'Isa. Two women in two very different houses, both remembered for a heart that stayed turned toward Allah, whatever the walls around it. So the child who will one day stand against Pharaoh grows up in Pharaoh's house, held by Pharaoh's wife. The rescue walked in through the front door.

If you pray, ask for a steady voice.

45.title: Home to his mother
45.hook: the baby refuses every nurse until his sister leads them to his own mother
45.howItsDone: Muslims often point to Musa's return to his mother as a sign that Allah's promises are kept, and teachers use the story with children to talk about trust.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Asiya's arms, and a queen who said do not kill him. Your line was a good heart in a hard house.
screen: `A GOOD HEART IN A HARD HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Back upstream, in a small house, a mother sits very still. She's set her son on the river, and the Qur'an is plain about what that costs: the heart of Musa's mother became empty. Hollowed out. So empty she nearly gave the whole secret away, and would have, the verse says, if Allah hadn't strengthened her heart. But she doesn't just sit. She turns to her daughter, Musa's sister, and gives her one word: follow him.
screen: `A HEART GONE EMPTY.` → `SHE NEARLY TELLS.` → `FOLLOW HIM.`

segments.voice: Surah al-Qasas keeps going. The sister watches from a distance, the Qur'an says, while they didn't notice her. Picture a girl at the edge of a crowd at the palace, trying to look like she's just passing by. Inside, there's a problem. The baby won't nurse. Nurse after nurse is brought in, and he turns away from every one. The Qur'an says Allah had forbidden him the foster mothers beforehand. So the sister sees her chance. She steps forward, as innocently as she can: shall I show you a household who will raise him for you and take good care of him? And so, the verse says, We returned him to his mother, so that her eye might be cooled, and she would not grieve, and so she would know that the promise of Allah is true. On day forty-three, at the river, she was promised: We will bring him back to you. Here it is, a few verses later. And yesterday's image is back too: her eye cooled, the same delight Asiya felt, now given to the woman who bore him. Notice who makes it happen. Not an army, not a miracle anyone can see. A baby who won't feed, and a sister brave enough to speak up at the right moment. The Qur'an doesn't give the sister's name, and says no more about her after this. But without her, no homecoming. Some commentators add that the mother was even paid to nurse her own son. The text itself only says he came home.
screen: `THE SISTER WATCHES FROM AFAR.` · `HE REFUSES EVERY NURSE.` · `SHALL I SHOW YOU A HOUSEHOLD?` · `THE PROMISE KEPT.` · then, large: `HER EYE COOLED.`

segments.voice: Think back for something you lost, let go of or gave up on that found its way back: a friendship that restarted after years, a thing misplaced for a month, a sense of humor after a bad season, your appetite for something you used to love. Notice who or what carried it home; often it's someone small, standing at the edge of the crowd. If you pray, give thanks for it.
Musa, the baby who refused every nurse until his sister brought him home, his mother's eye cooled at last.

46.title: The blow and the flight
46.hook: the grown Musa strikes a man who dies, repents at once, and flees Egypt
46.howItsDone: Muslims seek forgiveness with istighfar, asking Allah's pardon, often many times a day, and Musa's words "my Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me" are among the Qur'anic prayers people use.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Musa, home to his mother, and a promise kept. Your line was what is yours returns.

Everyone has a moment they'd give anything to take back. The angry text. The slammed door. It took a second, and it's lasted years. The baby from the river is a grown man now, given wisdom and knowledge, the Qur'an says. One day he walks into the city at an hour when nobody's paying attention, and finds two men fighting, one from his own people, one from Pharaoh's side. His man shouts for help. Musa steps in and strikes the other man, once. And the man falls, and doesn't get up.
screen: `THE SECOND YOU CAN'T TAKE BACK.` → `TWO MEN FIGHTING.` → `ONE BLOW.`

segments.voice: Look how fast Musa turns. In Surah al-Qasas, his words come right there over the body. First: this is of Satan's doing; he is an enemy, a clear misleader. Then, straight to Allah: my Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me. And the next words: so He forgave him. He is the Forgiving, the Merciful. Two sentences. No excuses about the fight, or who started it, or that he was only defending someone. The Arabic is zalamtu nafsi: I wronged my own self. In the Qur'an's way of seeing it, when you do wrong, the first person you injure is you. Muslim scholars generally explain that Musa never meant to kill; the word for the blow suggests a punch, a single strike with the fist. But he doesn't hide behind that. Then a promise: my Lord, because of the favor You've shown me, I will never be a helper to the guilty. The very next day, he's tested. The same man is fighting again, calling to him again. As Musa moves toward the other man, a voice cries out: Musa, do you mean to kill me, the way you killed a man yesterday? Then a man comes running from the far end of the city: the chiefs are plotting to kill you. Get out. I'm giving you good advice. And Musa leaves Egypt, afraid, watching over his shoulder, praying: my Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people. The prince of the palace walks into the desert with nothing. The Qur'an doesn't hide its prophets' worst moments. It shows what they did with them.
screen: `THIS IS OF SATAN'S DOING.` · `I HAVE WRONGED MYSELF.` · `SO HE FORGAVE HIM.` · `A RUNNING MAN: GET OUT.` · then, large: `ZALAMTU NAFSI.`

segments.voice: Let one moment come up, a small one is fine, when anger moved faster than you did; don't replay the argument or build the case for why you were right. Just see it, and say inside the plain version: I did that. If you pray, you can use Musa's words, my Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me; if you don't, simply own it for a while without an excuse.
Zalamtu nafsi: I have wronged my own self. What Musa said over the body, before he even asked for forgiveness.
Your line: my lord, I wronged myself. The short kind, no excuses attached. That's day forty-six.

47.title: Water at Madyan
47.hook: Musa waters two women's flock, then sits in the shade and prays: I am in need of whatever good You send
47.howItsDone: Musa's words from Surah al-Qasas, my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me, are a prayer Muslims use when looking for work, a home, or a way forward.

segments.voice: Yesterday: zalamtu nafsi, the blow and the flight, and a prophet who owned his wrong at once. Your line was my lord, I wronged myself.

New city, no job, no friends yet, phone at two percent, a bench, and no idea what happens next. That's roughly where Musa is. He has walked out of Egypt with nothing, down a long desert road, to a well at a place called Madyan. A whole crowd of shepherds is jostling there, watering their animals. Off to one side, two young women hold their sheep back, waiting. He asks what's wrong. They say: we can't water until the shepherds have gone, and our father is a very old man. He's exhausted, a stranger, a fugitive.
screen: `A STRANGER WITH NOTHING.` → `A CROWD AT THE WELL.` → `TWO WOMEN, WAITING.`

segments.voice: Surah al-Qasas tells it in a few words: so he watered their flock for them. No speech. No asking who they are or what's in it for him. He does the heavy thing in front of him and pushes through the crowd with their sheep. Then comes the part people remember. He turns away to the shade and prays: my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me. The word for in need is faqir, the ordinary Arabic word for poor. A man raised in Pharaoh's palace, sitting in the shade, telling Allah he's poor. He doesn't ask for a job, a wife, or a way home. Whatever good. And look at the order: he helps first, then asks. The help wasn't a bargain; the prayer isn't a bill. Then the good arrives, walking. One of the two women comes back, the Qur'an says, walking shyly: my father invites you, to reward you for watering for us. The old man hears his story and tells him: don't be afraid, you're safe from the wrongdoing people. One daughter says: father, hire him; the best one to hire is the strong and the trustworthy. By the end of the passage Musa has work, a home and a wife, for eight or ten years of shepherding. The Qur'an doesn't name the old man. Some commentators identify him with the prophet Shu'ayb; others say he was someone else. Whatever good. It came in the shape of a family.
screen: `SO HE WATERED FOR THEM.` · `I AM IN NEED OF ANY GOOD.` · `FAQIR — POOR, IN NEED.` · `THE GOOD COMES WALKING.` · then, large: `THE STRONG, THE TRUSTWORTHY.`

segments.voice: Think of one small, heavy thing you could do for someone, carry the groceries, move the chair, answer the email they're dreading, and picture doing it and walking away without waiting for thanks. Then sit, as if in shade, and let your shoulders drop. If you pray, you can use Musa's words, my Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me; if not, just sit empty-handed and notice that that's allowed.
Faqir, in need: what Musa called himself in prayer, after he'd watered the flock and asked for nothing specific.
Your line: in need of any good. Rest doesn't have to be earned first. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 47 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE FIRE ON THE MOUNTAIN.`

48.title: The fire on the mountain
48.hook: on the way home Musa sees a fire and goes to fetch a coal, and is spoken to in the sacred valley of Tuwa
48.carry: you are in a sacred valley
48.tomorrow: The staff and the shining hand
48.howItsDone: Muslims take off their shoes before entering a mosque or stepping onto a prayer space, and Musa is honored with the title Kalimullah, the one to whom Allah spoke.

segments.voice: Yesterday: faqir, water at Madyan, and a stranger who helped first and asked after. Your line was in need of any good.

A trip out for milk. A wrong turn down a street you didn't know. A borrowed ladder carried back to a neighbor. Errands are where a lot of stories start. Years have passed at Madyan. Musa has served his time and is traveling with his family, in the dark and the cold. Off on the side of a mountain, he sees a fire. He tells his family: wait here. Maybe I can bring you back a burning coal, or find someone there who can show us the way. He's going for a coal. That's all.
screen: `BIG MOMENTS START AS ERRANDS.` → `A FIRE ON THE MOUNTAINSIDE.` → `WAIT HERE.`

segments.voice: Surah Ta-Ha tells what happens when he gets there. He's called by name. O Musa. I am your Lord. So take off your sandals; you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa. And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed. Before the mission, before the signs, the first instruction is about his feet. Commentators have offered more than one reason: out of respect, the way you'd take off your shoes entering a home; or so he'd feel the holy ground directly, nothing between him and it. The Qur'an doesn't explain. It just asks. Then the heart of it: I am Allah; there is no god but Me. So worship Me, and establish the prayer for My remembrance. Before Pharaoh, before any rescue: who God is, and prayer. This is why Musa has a special title in Islam: Kalimullah, the one Allah spoke to. Surah an-Nisa says Allah spoke to Musa directly. Surah al-Qasas adds that the voice came from a tree, on the right side of the valley. Jews and Christians tell this moment too, as the burning bush in Exodus. Musa didn't climb that mountain looking for God. He was looking for a coal to keep his family warm, and directions home. The sacred valley was right there on his errand. He just had to stop, and take off his shoes.
screen: `O MUSA, I AM YOUR LORD.` · `TAKE OFF YOUR SANDALS.` · `WORSHIP ME, AND PRAY.` · `KALIMULLAH — THE ONE SPOKEN TO.` · then, large: `THE SACRED VALLEY OF TUWA.`

segments.voice: Take your shoes off if you can, socks are fine, and stand on whatever floor you're on: carpet, tile, kitchen linoleum, grass. Feel it under your feet; don't try to make the room holy, just treat it for a while as if it might be. If you pray, you can remember the words, there is no god but Allah; if not, simply stand, and let the ground be the ground.
Kalimullah, the one Allah spoke to: Musa's title, from the voice that called him out of the fire on the mountain.
Your line: you are in a sacred valley. It all started with a trip for a coal. Day forty-eight, done.

49.title: The staff and the shining hand
49.word: The staff and the shining hand
49.hook: his staff becomes a snake and his hand comes out white and shining: two signs
49.howItsDone: Muslims count the staff and the shining hand among the signs, ayat, given to Musa, and the story is often told to show how Allah works through ordinary things.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kalimullah, called from the fire on the mountain and told to take off his sandals. Your line was you are in a sacred valley. Today, the end of the week.

Look down at your hands. What's in them? A phone, probably. A coffee. A steering wheel, hopefully not. It's easy to stop noticing what you carry. Musa is still standing barefoot in the sacred valley. He's just been told who God is, and that he's been chosen. The next thing he hears isn't a thunderclap or a list of orders. It's a question, almost casual, the kind a friend asks, about the thing in his hand.
screen: `WHAT'S IN YOUR HANDS?` → `STILL BAREFOOT IN THE VALLEY.` → `A QUESTION, NOT AN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Surah Ta-Ha. In Pickthall's old translation: "And what is that in thy right hand, O Moses?" Of course Allah knows what it is. So why ask? Some commentators say it was to make Musa look closely at something ordinary, so he'd know exactly what it was before it changed. And Musa answers at length. It's my staff. I lean on it. I knock leaves down with it for my sheep. And I have other uses for it too. Some commentators smile at that long answer: a man just spoken to by his Lord, who doesn't want the conversation to end. Then: throw it down. He does, and it's a snake, moving fast. Take it, and don't be afraid; We'll return it to how it was. Then the second sign: put your hand under your arm, and it will come out white, without any harm. The Qur'an adds that phrase, and commentators read it as ruling out illness: light, not sickness. Two signs, both from what he already has. A shepherd's stick. His own hand. Nothing brought down from the sky. The ordinary thing, looked at properly, turns out to be enough for the mission. And that's the week. A mother's hands letting go of a chest. A queen's arms. A sister who spoke up. A blow Musa regretted. Water at a well. A fire on a mountain. And now a staff. Seven days, and most of the turning points were in someone's hands.

segments.voice: Look at what's in your hand, the phone or the cup, or your empty hand: turn it over, see the lines, the knuckles, the small scar you forgot you had. Then ask the question the way it was asked in the valley, what is this, and answer honestly, at length if you like, like Musa: what does it do for you, and what else could it be used for? If you pray, you can offer what's in your hand to Allah.
The staff and the shining hand: two signs, made from a shepherd's stick and his own hand.
